title:
Comment of Debra Ashton in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/28/2026

documents.name: 151872.txt
documents.text:
Debra Ashton, Montville, NJ.
I am 100% opposed to DeepGreen’s proposed underwater data center that is right in the middle of beluga whale habitat.  This habitat must be disturbed or destroyed.  Beluga whales are endangered (only an estimated 331 left in the Cook Inlet -- a 75% decline from their population in 1979), and they need all the protection we can give them.  An underwater data center would be detrimental to their survival.

Beluga whales are already competing with commercial shipping, port and coastal development, oil and gas exploration and production, and other anthropogenic activities, like fishing.

Belugas are among NOAA’s marine species at greatest near-term extinction risk.
A study published in Frontiers found that thermal discharge from power plants can alter oxygen and pH levels and sediment composition, which ultimately reduces the number and variety of creatures that live nearby and on the seabed.
These cumulative impacts coalescing is what spells trouble. NOAA identifies “cumulative and synergistic stressors" as a "high-concern threat" to beluga recovery.

Very importantly, belugas are echolocators, meaning they use a biological sonar system to “see” in Cook Inlet’s dark, icy waters. They rely on sound to communicate, navigate, find food, and detect danger, making underwater noise a serious concern for their survival and recovery.  A noisy data center would completely throw their sonar sense off.

DeepGreen’s proposed project could contribute to hearing impairment, separation of family groups, loss of prey or habitat, disruption of biologically important feeding and mating areas, physical injury, and behavioral changes. 

We cannot afford to make an already challenging environment even harsher for these belugas.

In a five-year review, NOAA actually reported that several anthropogenic noise sources were found at levels with the potential to chronically mask beluga communication and hearing, and that shipping and dredging sounds exceeded behavioral-harassment levels daily in some monitored settings.  And all that was determined BEFORE a 100-megawatt data center right in the middle of their critical habitat was proposed.

For an animal like the beluga, with only approximately 331 remaining in the Cook Inlet, the loss of even one Cook Inlet beluga whale should be considered devastating to the current population, as well as to the recovery of this magnificent species.

FERC needs to truthfully evaluate what this project adds to the belugas existing burden (and it's significant); not pretend it’s being developed in a vacuum.
